prompts.promptVerbatim: Know type I and Type II alveolar cells
prompts.supported: Type I cells provide alveolar structure. Type II cells secrete surfactant onto the inner alveolar surface. Keep these separate from alveolar macrophages, which ingest foreign material. The gas-exchange unit also includes respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Role of surfactant in the lungs-infants and adults
prompts.supported: Surfactant facilitates inflation during inspiration and lowers surface tension at end-expiration, opposing collapse. In premature infants, inadequate production and secretion cause widespread atelectasis and hypoventilation; shunting and hypoxemia follow. Surfactant deficiency therefore changes mechanics as well as gas exchange.

COPD includes airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. Tobacco smoke, occupational exposures and air pollution are listed COPD risks. The slide headed chronic bronchitis instead describes a self-limited viral illness; that conflicting block is not used as chronic-bronchitis teaching.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know gas exchange in the lungs
prompts.supported: Ventilation brings air into and out of the lungs. Diffusion carries oxygen across the thin alveolocapillary membrane into blood. Systemic perfusion delivers that blood to tissues, where oxygen diffuses into cells. Carbon dioxide follows the reverse direction. A large surface area, thin membrane and oxygen partial-pressure gradient support diffusion. Ventilation and perfusion must be distributed together.

prompts.promptVerbatim: How is the patient’s alveolar ventilation measured?
prompts.supported: Minute volume is breathing rate multiplied by air volume per breath. The deck assesses alveolar ventilation using arterial blood gases, specifically PaCO₂. Spirometry measures air volume and flow; it is a different measurement.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know asthma (adult and childhood)- pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, inflammatory mediators, clinical manifestations, treatment (acute and chronic), complications
prompts.supported: Asthma is chronic bronchial inflammation with hyperresponsiveness and variable reversible obstruction. Early attacks combine smooth-muscle contraction, edema and tenacious mucus. The late response starts 4–8 hours later with inflammatory-cell recruitment, impaired clearance and plugs; untreated inflammation can remodel the airway. Notes distinguish IL-13 effects on clearance, fibroblasts and constriction from IL-17 neutrophilic inflammation. Childhood asthma adds IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity and genetic/environmental influences. Expiratory wheeze, cough, dyspnea and prolonged expiration are typical; status asthmaticus resists usual measures. The packet lists oxygen, inhaled beta agonists, inhaled corticosteroids, immunotherapy, anti-IgE therapy, exposure education and peak-flow monitoring. Childhood medications use a stepwise approach.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Ageing and the pulmonary system
prompts.supported: Aging is associated with loss of elastic recoil, a stiffer chest wall, greater flow resistance and changes in gas exchange. Alveolar wall tissue and capillaries are lost. PaO₂, ventilatory reserve, respiratory muscle strength and endurance decrease, limiting exercise tolerance.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know how oxygen and CO2 is carried in the blood
prompts.supported: Oxygen binds hemoglobin to form oxyhemoglobin. A right shift means lower affinity and easier release to cells; the deck associates it with acidosis, hypercapnia and hyperthermia. A left shift increases affinity and inhibits tissue unloading; alkalosis, hypocapnia and hypothermia favor it. Carbon dioxide travels dissolved in plasma, as bicarbonate, and in carbamino compounds. The Haldane effect is named as the effect of oxygen on CO₂ transport.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know pulmonary edema: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: Excess lung water can result from altered capillary hydrostatic pressure, oncotic pressure or permeability. Left-heart disease is the most common cause listed. Postobstructive edema can follow relief of upper-airway obstruction and produces dyspnea, hypoxemia and greater work of breathing. The treatment overview targets the cause: cardiac output and volume for hydrostatic edema; removal of an injurious agent and supportive oxygenation for permeability edema. Oxygen or ventilation may be required; PEEP is listed for postobstructive edema.

prompts.promptVerbatim: How do different disease processes cause hypoxemia?
prompts.supported: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch is identified as the most common cause. Poor ventilation of perfused units and poor perfusion of ventilated units both impair effective exchange. Ventilated but unperfused alveoli are dead space. Thickening the exchange membrane or reducing its area impairs diffusion. Hypoventilation raises PaCO₂ and lowers available alveolar oxygen. The altitude explanation in the notes conflates inspired oxygen fraction with partial pressure; it is withheld.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know ARDS: pathophysiology, etiology, description, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: ARDS is acute inflammation with diffuse alveolocapillary injury. In the exudative phase within 72 hours, membrane damage increases permeability, edema develops and surfactant is inactivated. Proliferation at 4–21 days involves type II pneumocytes and fibroblasts; the fibrotic phase at 14–21 days involves remodeling, alveolar destruction and severe right-to-left shunting. The ranges overlap; they are not a rigid clock. Hypoxemia responds poorly to oxygen, and increasing work can progress to hypercapnia, acidosis and organ dysfunction. The deck lists ventilatory support, PEEP, low-volume ventilation and prone positioning. It also lists experimental-sounding therapies without separating them from routine treatment; those are not scored treatment recommendations.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know pulmonary hypertension: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, pressures, treatment, complications

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know viral/bacterial pneumonia in adults and children: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: Adult pneumonia is lower-respiratory infection; routes include aspiration, inhalation, airway equipment and bacteremia. Pneumococcal inflammation causes alveolar edema and consolidation. Adult findings include cough, dyspnea, fever, chills and pleuritic pain. Bacterial disease is treated with antibiotics; viral disease generally receives supportive therapy unless a secondary bacterial infection occurs. Pediatric viral pneumonia commonly involves RSV and destruction/sloughing of distal ciliated epithelium. Bacterial pediatric disease commonly involves streptococci or staphylococci and has higher temperature, neutrophils and bands than viral disease in the supplied comparison. Aspiration prevention, pulmonary hygiene and appropriate vaccination are listed.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know cystic fibrosis: pathophysiology, etiology, inheritary pattern, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: CF is an autosomal recessive multisystem disorder with abnormal chloride transport. Defective epithelial ion handling dehydrates airway mucus; thick secretions, impaired clearance and retained bacteria promote chronic inflammation. Neutrophil debris adds DNA and actin that increase viscosity. Consequences include bronchiectasis, pneumonia, hypoxia and fibrosis. Findings include persistent cough/wheeze, sputum, recurrent pneumonia and clubbing. The packet describes sweat chloride testing and newborn screening; care includes clearance techniques, aerosol therapies, antibiotics and nutritional support, including pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins.

prompts.supported: Croup is acute laryngotracheobronchitis with subglottic edema, usually infectious and usually viral in the notes. It commonly affects ages 6 months–5 years. Glucocorticoids are listed; severe cases may receive nebulized epinephrine and oxygen. Recurrent croup without infection symptoms may reflect underlying narrowing.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know tuberculosis: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an acid-fast bacillus transmitted by airborne droplets. Granulomatous tubercles and surrounding scar isolate bacilli; caseous necrosis develops. Infection can remain dormant or become active. Latent infection is asymptomatic; active manifestations include fatigue, weight loss, low-grade afternoon fever, night sweats and purulent cough. A positive skin test does not distinguish past, latent or active disease. The deck lists culture, immunoassays and imaging, and names isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know the anatomy of the kidney, how much cardiac output do the kidneys gets?
prompts.supported: Retroperitoneal kidneys have cortex outside and medulla inside. Cortex contains glomeruli and much of the convoluted tubules; medullary pyramids contain tubules and collecting ducts. Urine reaches minor calyces, major calyces, pelvis and ureter. Afferent arterioles supply glomeruli; efferent arterioles lead to a second capillary bed. The deck gives renal blood flow of 1000–1200 mL/min, plasma flow of 600–700 mL/min and filtration of about 20% of plasma flow. This last number is not the percentage of cardiac output.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Understand the RAAS system.
prompts.supported: Renin release is triggered by reduced afferent pressure/stretch, reduced distal sodium chloride or sympathetic stimulation, as described in the notes. Renin helps form angiotensin I; ACE converts it to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts vessels, stimulates adrenal aldosterone, promotes ADH secretion and thirst. The system increases pressure and sodium reabsorption.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know ADH, aldosterone and all renal hormones.
prompts.supported: ADH increases distal/collecting-duct water permeability, raising water reabsorption and lowering final urine volume. Aldosterone increases distal sodium absorption and supports potassium secretion by principal cells. ANP and BNP oppose sodium/water retention and inhibit renin/aldosterone; urodilatin and C-type peptide provide additional vascular/diuretic effects. Renalase supports catecholamine metabolism. Calcitriol supports intestinal calcium/phosphate absorption. Renal erythropoietin supports red-cell production.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know UTIs: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, most common “bugs”, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: UTI involves bacterial inflammation of urinary epithelium, commonly through retrograde ascent from gut flora. E. coli and Staphylococcus saprophyticus are named common pathogens. Uropathogen pili/fimbriae promote attachment and biofilms resist host defenses. Flow during voiding, acidic urine, uromodulin, uroepithelial secretions and closure of the ureterovesical junction help defend the tract. Symptoms and care depend on location; pediatric infection can present as unexplained fever or new incontinence.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know renal calculi (all types): pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: Formation progresses from supersaturation through precipitation to crystallization/agglomeration around a nidus. Calcium oxalate/phosphate, struvite, uric acid and inherited amino-acid-related stones are listed. Inadequate fluid intake is a major risk. Alkaline urine favors calcium phosphate; acidic urine favors uric acid. Staghorn describes a stone filling calyces, not its chemical composition. Renal colic is the characteristic manifestation. Management reduces stone-forming concentration, adjusts pH, controls pain and removes or fragments stones when needed.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know acute renal failure: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: AKI is a sudden fall in kidney function/GFR with nitrogenous waste accumulation. Prerenal injury begins with hypoperfusion; intrarenal injury affects parenchyma/interstitium, commonly ischemic ATN; postrenal injury follows obstruction of outflow. Treatment addresses fluids, electrolytes, pressure, infection and nutrition; severe disturbances may need dialysis.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know hemolytic uremic syndrome: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment, complications
prompts.supported: The packet links HUS to bacterial toxins including E. coli O157:H7. Endothelial injury, swelling and microthrombi obstruct glomerular vessels, lowering filtration. Care addresses hydration/nutrition, hypertension, potassium and seizures; dialysis and transfusion may be needed.
